# Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement

Soheil Abbasloo    Peng Cheng Affiliation: Microsoft Research

###### Abstract

A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and
deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models
give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We
show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a
capability in its own right — knowing when to hold a position and when
to yield to a better one — which we call _dialectical competence_. It
stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can
be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and
training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought
at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from
the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition
arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside,
we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the
model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest
case against that position — its _antithesis_ — rules on whether the
case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at
training or at deployment. We call this learning through
_Self-Disagreement_: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards
throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its
reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data
and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather
than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is
not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers
the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself.
The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not
come from outside it.

## 1 Introduction

Benchmarks do not talk back: Language models have become markedly better
at solving problems across successive open frontier
families ([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib11); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib48)), with reinforcement learning against answers a
program can check providing one route to that improvement ([DeepSeek-AI
et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib36); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib49); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). Benchmark suites
register that progress across general knowledge ([Hendrycks et al.,
2020](#bib.bib15)), graduate-level science ([Rein et al.,
2023](#bib.bib34)), competition mathematics ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib16); [Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)) and code ([Jain
et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)). Yet each ultimately reduces evaluation to a
question, a model’s answer, and a score on that answer. Deployment is
often different: users push back on assistants; inside agentic loops
another process may propose a different answer and contest a draft
before it is accepted ([Qian et al., 2023](#bib.bib33); [Hong et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17); [Wu et al., 2023](#bib.bib47)); and later turns may
ask a model to reconsider an answer it has already given. Disagreement
of that kind is not hostile and not an edge case; it is the normal
texture of use. Answers, however, move under it: models accommodate a
user’s stated view rather than the evidence ([Sharma et al.,
2023](#bib.bib37)), give up correct answers when merely doubted ([Laban
et al., 2023](#bib.bib22)), and abandon answers that were right under
sustained counter-reasoning ([Wang et al., 2023a](#bib.bib42)), at rates
that do not fall as the model gets stronger ([Abbasloo,
2025](#bib.bib1)).

Figure 1: Answering better does not buy the capability. Share of the
base model’s correct answers each arm gives up under challenge, one
position per challenger; each trained arm is the mean of three training
seeds. Each of the three ordinarily trained arms answers better on its
own and still tracks the base model here, as does SCoRe ([Kumar et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21);
App. [N](#A14 "Appendix N SCoRe, implemented as a trained baseline ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"));
only our design, Self-Disagreement (SelfD-RL), separates from them — by
25.3 pp on Qwen3-8B and 36.1 pp on Gemma-2 9B on average across these
eleven frontier challengers (up to 45 and 67 pp from the base model;
more in
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

A capability in its own right: What moves under challenge is not another
shortfall in answering, because the failure begins after a correct
answer has already been produced. What is missing is the ability to
weigh a case made against a position and to adjust only when the case
deserves it — holding when the challenge is incorrect, yielding when it
is correct — which we call _dialectical competence_. Training for
correctness does not supply it, though correctness is its precondition:
a model that cannot reach the right answer has nothing to hold. It is
the higher skill, standing on answering rather than competing with it.
It is also the capability hard to supply from outside, because every way
of correcting a model that leans on a stronger judge — a larger model, a
separate verifier, a person — needs that judge to exist, and one better
than the model being corrected is rare and costly. To separate the two,
we train on two base models drawn from different families,
Qwen3-8B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib48)) and Gemma-2 9B ([Gemma Team
et al., 2024](#bib.bib9)), and run the same comparison on each.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
places the base model beside three ordinarily trained arms (each defined
in
§[B](#A2 "Appendix B Reproduction and artifacts ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
against the same challengers: each answers better on its own, and each
still gives up its correct answers under challenge at close to the base
model’s rate. Training against the model’s own opposition separates from
that pattern, on both families (the diagnosis is made precise in
§[2](#S2 "2 The problem ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Our proposal — learning through Self-Disagreement: The remedies that
suggest themselves share one defect: every one of them works on the
answer, when the capability at issue is the further one that begins
after the answer. Training harder for correctness, giving the model a
second pass over its own answer, and training it to judge that answer
before committing all track the base model rather than separating from
it
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"));
buying more inference — a reconsideration pass, or sampling many answers
and voting — does not reach it either
(§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"));
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Related work ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
discusses these lines of work at greater length. In each, the move the
model makes is prompted, sampled or borrowed; it never follows from the
model’s own ruling on a case it was made to confront. The dialectical
tradition puts exactly that ruling at the center: a position is
developed by meeting the strongest case against it ([Plato,
1963](#bib.bib31); [Popper, 2005](#bib.bib32)); that case is raised from
within the position rather than handed to it from above ([Hegel,
2018](#bib.bib14)); and the position must rule on the case before it may
move. We take this as a training paradigm rather than as a metaphor. A
single policy plays both parts, differing only in what each is shown. It
states a position, the _thesis_; in a context of its own, holding the
question and the case just made but never the reference answer, it
argues against that position, the _antithesis_; it then returns to the
answering role, rules on whether that case stands, and commits to a
final answer, the _synthesis_
(§[3](#S3 "3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Only the answering turns are rewarded, and the reward is the verifier we
already have: the same check that scores an answer against its reference
also scores the answer the model settles on once opposed. No reward
model, no preference data, no second model at training or deployment:
_the opposition a model needs, it supplies itself_. We contribute:

1.  (1)
    _Dialectical competence as a capability in its own right_: we
    measure it on a probe built for it, and show that neither
    accuracy-centered training nor inference-time remedies supply it
    (§[2](#S2 "2 The problem ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
2.  (2)
    _Self-Disagreement_: a single-policy extension of RLVR, with the
    opposition drawn from the policy being trained
    (§[3](#S3 "3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
3.  (3)
    _Demonstrating that Self-Disagreement improves it_: trained on two
    base families, the models gain dialectical competence without paying
    for it in first-answer accuracy
    (§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
    and keep the gain against challengers they never trained against,
    with an account of where it comes from
    (§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

## 2 The problem

A probe that makes holding and yielding visible: Benchmarks record
whether a model ended up right, not what it did when it was pushed, so
we measure on a probe built for the second question. We call it the
_disagreement probe_, or _D-probe_, and it is used for every measurement
of behavior under challenge in this paper. It is 327 questions, each put
to every one of 17 challengers — 15 external models spanning open
checkpoints to frontier systems, the model’s own frozen starting point,
and its own critique. The diagnosis below runs it on the two base
models, Qwen3-8B and Gemma-2 9B. Every model answers once and that
answer is replayed to each challenger, so only the answer given after
the challenge can differ, and all three answers are graded: the model’s
own, the challenger’s, and the one the model settles on. Knowing which
of the first two was right is what makes that choice legible, because it
says what the right action was. What we report is the accuracy of that
settled answer, the _synthesis accuracy_.

The label is checked, not assumed: Synthesis accuracy is what the metric
rests on, so it was checked a second way: on the items where a base
model gives up a correct answer, a blinded jury of Claude-Opus-4.7,
GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-pro-preview reads the reasoning and judges all
121 such items to be non-genuine — conceding and adopting the
challenger’s answer with no valid pushback, or merely restating it —
rather than a differently argued answer. What synthesis accuracy loses
is therefore reasoning under challenge, not a relabelled answer
(§[G](#A7 "Appendix G Construct validation of the primary metric ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Both base models are one-sided: What their synthesis accuracy is made
of, rather than its level, is the diagnosis. On the items where the
model was right and the challenger wrong — where holding is the correct
action — Qwen3-8B ends on the correct answer 53.3 % of the time and
Gemma-2 9B 25.1 %. On the items where the challenger was right and the
model wrong, where yielding is correct, the same two models score 84.1 %
and 93.2 %. That pairing is not discrimination between good arguments
and bad; it is close to unconditional surrender, and one behavior
produces both numbers. The cost rises with the challenger: across
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")’s
challengers the base model gives up 17 % to 61 % of its correct answers
on Qwen3-8B and 25 % to 83 % on Gemma-2 9B.

Figure 2: Buying accuracy is not buying the capability. SuperGPQA: each
arm sits at its thesis accuracy ($`x`$) against how often it gave up a
correct answer under challenge ($`y`$, inverted), so better is up and to
the right. Bars are $`\pm 1`$ sd across three training seeds (for Base,
over its eight sampled answers).

Training for accuracy does not reach it: The natural reading of that is
that the models are not yet good enough, and that better answering will
carry the rest. It does not. A control trained for accuracy alone
(Accuracy-RL; defined, with its settings, in
§[B](#A2 "Appendix B Reproduction and artifacts ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
from the same base model and the same data, also improves the first
answer and buys none of the behavior under challenge, which can drift
against it over training rather than holding steady
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E The reward ablation, and the same dissociation within one arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 The problem ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows it on SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)): the
trained alternatives, the published self-correction method SCoRe ([Kumar
et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) among them, move right, to higher thesis
accuracy, and stay at the same height. Answering well is the floor, not
the capability: a model that cannot produce the right answer has none to
hold, but past that floor more of it buys nothing here. Nor is the
opposition’s content incidental: an opposition that carries no content
recovers only part of the gain
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

What that leaves: The failure is not a shortfall that better answering
removes, and it is not repaired by the inference-time remedies we test,
self-consistency ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib44)) and
self-reflection ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib30)), or by training the
same objective harder. What is missing is the decision itself: telling a
correct challenge from an incorrect one and acting on the difference.
The rest of this paper is about training that.

## 3 Design

Overview: We train a single policy under a dialectical protocol we call
_Self-Disagreement_. The policy commits to an answer, argues against
that answer in a separate context, then returns to rule on the argument
before committing again. Only the answering turns are trained. The
protocol extends RLVR rather than departing from it: the verifier that
scores an answer against its reference also scores the ruling, and
nothing else in the training loop changes.

Where the opposition comes from: Learning to adjudicate disagreement
presupposes a source of disagreement. The usual construction takes it
from a second model, which makes the training signal a property of the
_pair_: an opposition that is too weak can be dismissed without
discrimination, and one that is too strong makes deference the best
available response. The policy’s competence also changes as it trains,
so a pairing calibrated at the start does not stay calibrated, and
keeping it so means tracking a quantity that is not directly observable.
Drawing the opposition from the policy itself removes that coupling. Its
competence tracks the policy’s by construction and without scheduling,
every training item has an opposition available without a second model
to serve it, and what is deployed is a single set of weights. The
construction does rest on an assumption worth stating: that a policy can
be induced to argue against a position it has just committed to.

The dialectical exchange:
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows one exchange and
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
one training step; the prompt templates for all three turns are printed
verbatim in
§[C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement").
The policy is prompted into two roles that share its weights and differ
only in what each is shown. In the answering role it writes the
_thesis_, and later the _synthesis_; in the opposing role it writes the
_antithesis_, disputing the strategy, the decisions and the reasoning of
that particular answer _even where they appear correct_ rather than
making an independent second attempt at the question. Opposition is
therefore unconditional — a correct thesis is argued against as readily
as an incorrect one — which is what makes _holding_ a position something
the policy must learn, since a policy opposed only when it was wrong
would never need to tell a sound challenge from an unsound one. Let
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ be the policy and let $`q\sim\mathcal{D}`$ be a
question with reference answer $`y^{\star}`$. One dialectical exchange
is a trajectory $`\tau=(T,A,S)`$ of three generations from the _same_
parameters under two role prompts — answering, then opposing, then
answering again under instruction to judge:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\pi_{\theta}(\tau\mid q)\;=\;\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(T\mid q)}_{\text{thesis}}\;\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(A\mid q,T)}_{\text{antithesis (sampled, inference-only)}}\;\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(S\mid q,T,A)}_{\text{synthesis}},
``` |  | (1) |

The synthesis $`S`$ is internally ordered: it opens with a verdict
$`v\in\{0,1\}`$ on $`A`$’s answer and only then commits to an answer.
Because the answer is decoded after the verdict and conditioned on it,
the policy must adjudicate before it may answer, and $`v`$ is separately
verifiable; ablating the verdict removes that opening block, leaving a
synthesis that answers with no obligation to rule. Writing
$`\mathcal{V}(\cdot\,;y^{\star})\in\{0,1\}`$ for the ordinary RLVR
verifier — exact match against the reference answer, so that no learned
reward model and no preference data enter anywhere — the trajectory
induces $`c_{T}=\mathcal{V}(T;y^{\star})`$,
$`c_{S}=\mathcal{V}(S;y^{\star})`$, and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
c_{v}\;=\;\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,v=\mathcal{V}(A;y^{\star})\,\right],
``` |  | (2) |

which scores whether the policy judged the opposition rightly, not
whether the opposition was right. This is where the verifier’s reach is
extended: the same check, applied to a decision about the opposition’s
answer rather than to an answer. The credit is available on every item,
including those in which the opposition concedes, so the objective by
itself does not rule out a policy that agrees whenever the opposition
agrees with it. It is more than that: removing the content of the
disagreement, together with the supervision that depends on that
content, costs roughly half to two thirds of the gain, and the trained
policy keeps its advantage against challengers it never trained against
(§[F](#A6 "Appendix F What the opposition and the verdict do in training ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The antithesis is sampled from the policy but is *inference-only*: its
trajectory is never collected into the training episode, so
$`\pi_{\theta}(A\mid q,T)`$ is a sampling distribution rather than an
optimized factor, and opposing is never rewarded — only answering and
adjudicating are — which removes any route by which it could learn to
soften its challenges. No factor of
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In 3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"))
is conditioned on $`y^{\star}`$: the verifier is applied only after the
trajectory is complete, so it cannot oppose selectively on items it is
about to answer incorrectly. Thesis and synthesis are optimized as one
trajectory, not as separate turns, so credit assignment reaches the
answer and the ruling on its challenge jointly.

Guarding against collapse: The characteristic failure of an endogenous
construction is trivial agreement, in which $`A`$ concedes $`T`$ and the
dialectic degenerates to a single pass. Two provisions address this,
neither of them part of the objective. The first is uninformedness,
above: the opposing role cannot tell which items it would be safe to
concede. The second is the admission band — items enter training only
when the base policy’s pass rate
$`p_{0}(q)=\Pr[\mathcal{V}(T;y^{\star})=1\mid q;\pi_{\theta_{0}}]`$ lies
in $`[\underline{p},\overline{p}]`$, which excludes items on which
opposition is respectively vacuous or futile. What the opposition and
the verdict actually do in training is then an empirical question rather
than a guaranteed one, and we treat it as such:
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F What the opposition and the verdict do in training ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
measures the opposition the policy actually produces, and
§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
measures the resulting behavior rather than relying on the construction.

At inference: None of the training machinery is required to use the
result. The trained policy is an ordinary model: it answers a question
in one pass, and what training has changed is how it behaves *when it is
disagreed with*. The evaluation of
§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
therefore presents the trained policy with an opposing view and measures
the answer it commits to, the same situation the protocol trains, with
none of the environment’s apparatus. There is no admission band, no
candidate selection, no verifier and no reference answer, and, since the
opposing role is the policy itself, no second model to deploy.

The objective: Two failures are penalized directly:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\underbrace{\mathbf{1}[\,c_{T}=1,\;c_{S}=0\,]}_{\mathrm{cap}\;\text{(capitulation)}}\qquad\underbrace{\mathbf{1}[\,c_{T}=0,\;\mathcal{V}(A;y^{\star})=1,\;c_{S}=0\,]}_{\mathrm{stub}\;\text{(stubbornness)}}
``` |  | (3) |

Capitulation is a correct thesis surrendered; stubbornness is a valid
challenge refused. *Synthesis accuracy*, $`\Pr(c_{S}{=}1)`$, is the
outcome variable of every result in this paper. The return, for the
configuration reported throughout, is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(\tau)\;=\;\beta\,c_{S}\;+\;w_{v}c_{v}\;+\;w_{T}c_{T}\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{cap}}\,\mathrm{cap}\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{stub}}\,\mathrm{stub}\;-\;w_{\phi}\big(\phi_{T}+\phi_{v}\big),
``` |  | (4) |

subject to a hard format gate: if either the thesis or the verdict fails
to parse ($`\phi_{T}\vee\phi_{v}`$), the return is *replaced* by a floor
value and every positive channel is discarded,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(\tau)\;\leftarrow\;R_{\mathrm{floor}}\quad\text{if }\phi_{T}\vee\phi_{v}.
``` |  | (5) |

Here $`\lambda_{\mathrm{cap}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{stub}}=0.5`$,
$`w_{T}=1`$, $`w_{v}=0.4`$, $`w_{\phi}=0.1`$ and
$`R_{\mathrm{floor}}=-0.75`$. The objective keeps paying for a correct
first answer at full weight while adding the ruling at $`0.4`$: the
capability is trained on top of answering, not in place of it. The gate
is worth more than its weight suggests: the policy cannot decline to
adjudicate. The remaining coefficient, $`\beta`$, multiplies the
synthesis credit rather than adding to it: $`\beta=2.0`$ when
$`c_{T}=0`$ and $`\mathcal{V}(A;y^{\star})=0`$, and $`1`$ otherwise,
since that is the one cell where no correct position exists to defer to
and the answer has to be reached rather than chosen. The symmetry of
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{cap}}`$ and $`\lambda_{\mathrm{stub}}`$ is
load-bearing. An objective on terminal correctness alone is invariant to
the trajectory by which correctness is reached, including trajectories
that discard a correct answer and recover it — which
§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows accuracy-only training does not merely tolerate but increasingly
takes. Penalizing capitulation alone would buy stability at the cost of
revisability. Optimization is by GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)):
for each $`q`$ a group of $`G`$ trajectories is sampled and scored by
its group-relative advantage
$`\hat{A}_{i}=(R(\tau_{i})-\mu_{q})/\sigma_{q}`$, maximized under a
clipped surrogate ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib35)), with the KL
penalty to the reference policy applied to the return rather than to the
loss. The algorithm is unmodified: the dialectic changes what is scored,
not how the update is computed.

## 4 Evaluation

This section has three parts. The first asks whether the capability is
there at all, and whether available approaches produce it: it is weak in
the base model, arrives with training, holds on benchmarks the training
never saw, and no rival design or test-time scheme we compare reaches
it. The second asks where the gain comes from: whether the model answers
better on the first attempt or decides better once challenged, and which
part of the design buys it. The third asks whether the result is valid
and generalizes: a second reading of the metric by a blinded jury of
three frontier models, a different base model, and challengers it never
trained against.

Setup: Every trained arm is reinforcement learning from verifiable
rewards on the same data, from the same initialization and with the same
verifier; what separates them is the return and the number of turns it
is computed over. Two further arms are not trained at all: the test-time
schemes, which spend additional inference on the base model instead.
Every arm, the base model included, meets the challenge under the same
instruction, which asks for a verdict on it before the final answer;
without that request the other arms do no better, and on Qwen3-8B worse
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Because the opposition is sampled rather than fixed we resample it over
independent draws (eight; four in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"));
in the main comparisons each trained arm is the mean of three training
seeds and its spread is across seeds, the base model’s across its draws.
Capitulation and stubbornness, defined in
§[3](#S3 "3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
are counted over every scored item rather than over the subset on which
each could occur, so that they add to synthesis accuracy and to each
other. Behavior under challenge is measured on the D-probe throughout;
the benchmark panel asks whether what it measures survives away from it.
What each arm is, the model, data, hardware and optimizer settings, the
step at which each arm is read, and the construction of the disagreement
probe are in
§[B](#A2 "Appendix B Reproduction and artifacts ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement").

### 4.1 Overall results and analysis

Does it work, and could anything already available have done it: The
capability is not present in either base model and it arrives with
training in both
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The single-pass accuracy-trained arm (Accuracy-RL) is flat over its own
run, so more training compute does not close the gap; nor does spending
more at inference (the test-time columns of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
then asks whether what was learned on the probe survives away from it.

Figure 4: Dialectical competence is trained under Self-Disagreement,
while the arms that drop the disagreement recover at most part of it.
Bands across seeds. Separate models: read the shapes, not the cells.

It survives off the training probe, on both base models: On Qwen3-8B the
trained model is ahead of the base model on all nine public benchmarks,
on mathematics and code as well as on the multiple-choice sets where a
challenge is cheapest to issue, and on average it settles on the right
answer after being challenged +5.90 pp more often (95 % CI over the nine
benchmarks $`[+4.64,+7.16]`$; over the three training seeds
$`[+5.00,+6.80]`$), 50.0 % to 55.9 %. The final row of the upper block
of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
repeats the whole exercise on a second base model, Gemma-2 9B, and the
pattern holds: 19.9 % to 37.8 % on average, ahead of its own base on
every benchmark
(§[L](#A12 "Appendix L The second base model, benchmark by benchmark ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Every column of the upper block is read under the same protocol and
scored by the same verifier, so what separates the columns is what each
was trained to do and not how each was measured.

How it works with external challengers: The upper block of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
lets each arm meet its own antithesis, which is how the model is used;
the lower block holds the challenge fixed, giving every arm the same
first answer and the same antithesis from Gemini-3.8-flash or
Claude-Haiku-4.5, so that only the decision is the arm’s own
(App. [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The lead survives, 6.2 to 14.1 points over the base model with every
95 % interval over training seeds above 5, while no other arm, trained
on another objective or given more inference, gains more than 1.4 points
on it, and the reason lies in how each responds to the same challenge:
the other arms take most antitheses put to them, right or wrong, much as
the base model does, whereas Self-Disagreement holds a right first
answer against a wrong antithesis more than twice as often as any of
them and still takes most of the right ones. Nor does it win by
switching less: where the base model, its final answer biased toward its
first, switches as rarely as Self-Disagreement, it still trails it by
7.5 and 4.4 points of synthesis accuracy on Gemma-2 9B, one per outside
challenger
(App. [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
so what training on the challenge adds is which items the model holds
on, not how many, which is what telling a correct challenge from an
incorrect one looks like once the challenge itself is the same for
everyone.

Why none of the alternatives reach it:
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
sets six of them beside ours, and each falls short for its own reason.
Giving the base model more inference — Majority Vote over 64 samples an
item, or Test-Time Self-Reflection asking it once to review its answer —
buys more attempts but no one to disagree with, so what is missing is
not compute. Revise-RL trains a second pass, rewarded on the answer it
settles on and penalized for abandoning a correct one, but with nothing
disagreeing with it there is no valid challenge to refuse, so what is
missing is not the opportunity to change the answer. Verify-RL supplies
the verdict by having the model judge its own answer first, and rewards
the judgment alongside the answer; it comes closest of the four and
still recovers at most about half of our gain on both base models: a
verdict a model issues against itself is not the same as being argued
with. SCoRe ([Kumar et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), while better than either
on the panel, recovering more than half of our gain on both base models,
leaves capitulation where the base model has it
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The sixth is the arm built to maximize the quantity our result might be
mistaken for: Accuracy-RL trains on the same data with the same
verifier, differing only in taking a single pass rewarded on whether
that answer is right; its interval on the panel includes zero on
Qwen3-8B, and on Gemma-2 9B it gains 3.2 points, under a fifth of ours.
Optimizing the first answer does not deliver the capability as a
by-product, which it would have to for our gain to be better answers,
not better judgment — what a model carries into the dialectic and what
survives it are separable, and a model can reach a right answer and
still not distinguish it from a wrong one — though not the reverse,
since a model that cannot reach it has nothing to distinguish.

The same dissociation in the reward ablation: Holding the exchange fixed
and varying only what is returned moves the dialectical quantity several
times further than it moves accuracy: across the reward ablation, one
training seed per arm, the arms span 12.23 pp in synthesis accuracy
against 2.75 pp in thesis accuracy — 4.4 times as far — and the ordering
is not a trade. The same separation also appears within one arm over
training
(§[E](#A5 "Appendix E The reward ablation, and the same dissociation within one arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

### 4.2 Where the gain comes from

Synthesis accuracy rises, but it does not say why, and two mechanisms
would raise it equally: the model may answer better on the first attempt
and so meet fewer challenges it deserves to lose, or its dialectical
competence may itself have improved. Grading its first answer against
its challenger’s sorts every item into four situations by which side was
right. Writing $`\pi_{m}`$ for the share of items in situation $`m`$ and
$`r_{m}`$ for how often the model ends on the correct answer there,
synthesis accuracy is $`c_{S}=\sum_{m}\pi_{m}r_{m}`$, and the change
against the base model splits without remainder into a *situations* term
and a *skill* term,
$`\Delta c_{S}=\sum_{m}\Delta\pi_{m}\,r^{\mathrm{base}}_{m}+\sum_{m}\pi^{\mathrm{arm}}_{m}\,\Delta r_{m}`$,
the standard composition-versus-rate decomposition ([Kitagawa,
1955](#bib.bib20)), where *situations*, the first term, is what the
model gains by walking into a different mix of predicaments — the
better-first-answer explanation, the floor — and *skill*, the second, is
the part of the gain due to a change in dialectical competence, the
capability standing on that floor rather than an alternative to it. We
decompose it on the D-probe, over the same seventeen challengers;
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
gives the full profile and the reference policies.

Table 2: Only Self-Disagreement gains *skill*; the other arms gain only
*situations*. *Situations* is what an arm gains by walking into an
easier mix of predicaments — a better first answer; *skill* is what it
gains by handling the same predicament better. Points of synthesis
accuracy on the D-probe; for each arm the two terms sum to its total
change. Brackets are 95 % intervals clustered by question; each trained
arm is averaged over three training seeds, and its bracket is that
average’s. The base model is the reference.

Every arm improves its first answer; only Self-Disagreement also
improves the decision:
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
gives the split, and
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
the four situations behind it. The base models are one-sided — holding
only 53.3 % and 25.1 % of the time while yielding 84.1 % and 93.2 %,
which is closer to unconditional surrender than to discrimination.
Self-Disagreement holds 88.9 % and 89.5 % and still yields 53.3 % and
55.4 %, and that registers as skill: 11.08 of its 12.3-point gain on
Qwen and 14.83 of 15.4 on Gemma, positive against at least sixteen of
the seventeen challengers individually in every training seed of both
families. A model deciding no better than the base scores zero; one
deciding correctly in every situation it met would score 35.2 on Qwen
and 47.4 on Gemma. The trained rivals behave alike and oppositely: each
gains through situations, and none has a skill term above zero. SCoRe
gains no skill either: $`-1.29`$ on Qwen and $`+0.17`$ on Gemma, neither
interval above zero.

Figure 5: The content of the disagreement matters. Average over the nine
benchmarks and three training seeds (dots), each scored on eight sampled
answers. Bars are the gain over the base model, with 95 % CIs.

Does the disagreement have to be genuine, and does it have to come from
elsewhere: Two variants of the recipe answer this, each removing one
ingredient;
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
places them beside the full recipe. Content-Agnostic Disagreement
(CAD-RL) runs the same exchange against a challenge that does not depend
on the answer it challenges, and it reaches +2.70 $`[+1.66,+3.73]`$,
roughly a third to a half of the full recipe’s gain across training
seeds; its best seed stays 2.5 points below the full recipe’s weakest.
The presence of opposition carries part of the gain, and the rest
requires the opposition to be about something, which is also what makes
the verdict on it checkable
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
External Disagreement (ExtD-RL) is our own recipe with the antithesis
drawn from Qwen3-14B, a larger model of the same family, and it reaches
+5.09 $`[+3.66,+6.53]`$ against +5.90 for the policy arguing with
itself: a larger model’s opposition adds nothing over the policy’s own.
What separates them is less what they achieve than what they require:
the external arm holds a second model in service for the whole of
training, on a serving allocation held in a one-to-four ratio against
the one training used, and it leaves the choice of that model
unresolved, since it was picked for being larger than the model being
trained and we know of no principled way to make that choice. Both are
reported on Qwen3-8B only: they vary the *design* rather than ablate
ours, so neither is needed to establish that the effect reproduces on a
second base model. One might object that both arms argue inside our own
loop, so the model may only handle its own objections. It cannot be: the
advantage holds against almost every one of the fifteen challengers it
never trained against, several stronger than itself
(Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Which part of the design does the work: training against an opposition
with the answer given after it rewarded, with a further gain from paying
for a correct ruling; a second pass with nothing to rule on adds none of
it. Of the arms in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
only the two whose answer after the challenge is rewarded bring
capitulation below the base model’s 10.3 %; none of the others does,
SCoRe included, nor the exchange whose final answer goes unpaid.

Two further ablations separate the verdict from the opposition
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Requiring the verdict in the output but paying nothing for getting it
right gives $`2.9\pm 0.9`$ %, against $`1.0\pm 0.3`$ % for the full
recipe — a resolved gap of 1.9 pp, separating the *structural*
requirement from the reward for meeting it. A second pass with nothing
to rule on does not substitute: Revise-RL abandons its correct answer on
$`15.0\pm 2.4`$ % of all scored items, 14.0 pp from the full recipe, and
places it beside the unrewarded-dialectic and Accuracy-RL arms, none of
which is rewarded for an answer given after a challenge. The same reward
creates an obvious exploit, since it pays for correcting a flawed first
answer, and
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Reward-hacking controls ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
reports the controls: the rate at which the final answer simply
reproduces the challenger’s falls from 0.693 in the unrewarded-dialectic
arm to 0.393–0.419 in the arms that pay for the verdict, and the arm
with the verdict removed sits at 0.705, with the control not the
treatment.

### 4.3 Validity and generalization

Is the metric measuring what we claim: As
§[2](#S2 "2 The problem ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
reports, a blinded jury of three frontier models reads the reasoning and
finds what the metric counts to be a real failure rather than an
artifact of comparing two answer strings.
§[G](#A7 "Appendix G Construct validation of the primary metric ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
gives the validation in full — the rubric, the panel, the blinding, the
agreement statistics, and the limits of what this grading establishes.

|  | capitulation $`\downarrow`$ |  | synthesis $`\uparrow`$ |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model | base | + SelfD-RL | base | + SelfD-RL |
| Gemma 3 12B | $`20.2\pm 2.6`$ | $`\mathbf{2.6\pm 0.8}`$ | $`53.0\pm 1.9`$ | $`\mathbf{68.1\pm 0.8}`$ |
| Granite 3.1 8B | $`14.7\pm 1.3`$ | $`\mathbf{0.9\pm 0.8}`$ | $`40.5\pm 1.6`$ | $`\mathbf{46.1\pm 1.6}`$ |
| Llama 3.1 8B | $`6.6\pm 0.6`$ | $`\mathbf{2.6\pm 0.3}`$ | $`51.4\pm 1.7`$ | $`\mathbf{57.9\pm 0.7}`$ |
| Qwen3 14B^(‡) | $`1.8\pm 0.4`$ | $`\mathbf{0.8\pm 0.4}`$ | $`71.1\pm 0.7`$ | $`\mathbf{73.4\pm 0.6}`$ |

Table 4: The same recipe on other models, other sizes, and other
families. Before training and at convergence, mean $`\pm`$ sd over two
training seeds (%). ^(‡)Qwen3 14B was pre-registered as a near-null
because it begins with almost no headroom to move; it is reported for
that reason.

The gain holds against challengers that cannot have decayed: When the
model argues with itself, thesis and antithesis are the same checkpoint,
so a rise in synthesis accuracy could mean the model holds better or
that its own antithesis got worse. Separating the two needs a challenger
that does not move with the arm, and the ladder is built from them:
sixteen of the seventeen antithesis models are served from fixed weights
and are identical for every arm, so nothing an arm learns can change who
argues with it. Two of those sixteen are the base checkpoints the arms
were trained from — the frozen base models, each family’s own starting
point held still and replayed — which is the sharpest form of the test,
since it is the one challenger the arm might be suspected of having left
behind. Scoring synthesis accuracy on the same D-probe, with each
model’s own first answer frozen and replayed: against the frozen
Qwen3-8B the trained model reaches 73.2 % where its base reaches 60.5 %;
against the frozen gemma-2-9b-it, 57.7 % against 30.9 %. Those gains,
12.7 and 26.8 pp, are as large as the ones measured against the model’s
own antithesis, which is what rules the alternative reading out: a
decaying antithesis cannot explain a gain that survives almost every one
of the fifteen challengers that never changed.

Across other model families and sizes: The result is not a property of
one base model. Applying the same recipe to four further models — other
sizes and other families — synthesis accuracy rises and capitulation
falls in every one, whether or not its first answers improve, on the
same held-out items scored before and after training. All four end below
5 %, and three of them started above it
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Validity and generalization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Does it depend on who argues:
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
puts both models against every antithesis we ran, from a 4B model to the
strongest frontier systems available, including the base model itself
and a base model of the same size. Over much of that ladder the base
model would have done better by ignoring the antithesis entirely —
keeping its first answer, or taking the challenger’s, whichever is
stronger — and at worst it gives up 17.6 pp that way on Qwen3-8B; its
accuracy swings 26.5 pp from one end of the ladder to the other (45.4 on
Gemma-2 9B). Self-Disagreement falls short of its own reference by at
most 2.6 on Qwen3-8B, and swings 11.1 (20.0 on Gemma-2 9B). Whatever it
is arguing with, it ends up in much the same place, and that difference
between the two spans is large enough that no rung on the ladder
reverses it. A fixed-population measurement with different challengers
finds the same invariance
(§[H](#A8 "Appendix H What the trained model leaves on the table, across challengers ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

A model that ignores the exchange scores exactly one; neither of ours
does: For every item on which one of the thesis and the antithesis was
right and the other wrong, we ask whether the model ended up on the side
the evidence favored. Such a policy holds just as often when holding is
wrong as when it is right, so its two odds are equal and its ratio is
exactly one, whatever mix of items it meets. Neither model is near that.
On the same probe and the same seventeen antitheses as
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
the odds are 6.0 for the base model against 9.1 for the trained one on
Qwen3-8B, and 4.6 against 10.6 on Gemma-2 9B. SCoRe’s are 6.0 on
Qwen3-8B and 3.7 on Gemma-2 9B. Read antithesis by antithesis,
Self-Disagreement’s ratio is above one against all seventeen antitheses
on both base models once its three training seeds are pooled, the lowest
being 4.3 $`[3.7,5.0]`$ on Qwen3-8B and 2.4 $`[1.4,4.1]`$ on Gemma-2 9B.
Where a single seed falls short, the challenger is among the weakest —
small local models, including the base model itself — where holding is
the right move on about nine items in ten and the deciding cell holds
seven to twenty-three items. Those exceptions are lower bounds: a model
that swapped one wrong answer for another scores as having held, pushing
the ratio down. Here each model meets its own theses, so each ratio is
read against the null of one; given the base model’s exchange instead,
Self-Disagreement’s log odds ratio is above the base model’s and every
other arm’s
(App. [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

## 5 Limitations and concluding remarks

What we have not established: The recipe is trained on two base models
from different families and applied unchanged to four further models
across other sizes and families, where capitulation falls in every one.
That is evidence that the effect reproduces, not that it is universal:
establishing it across model families and scales in general would take a
far wider sweep than the compute here allows, and we do not claim it.
The same bound applies to the domain. Every reward here comes from
exact-match verification against a reference answer, so our evidence
covers only checkable answers; whether the same signal can be built
where correctness is not checkable is open. Every dialectical exchange
in the main text is also a single round of challenge; three rounds are
in
§[P](#A16 "Appendix P Repeated challenge ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement").

How far there is still to go: Self-Disagreement moves the decision
itself, but it does not finish the job. Its skill term reaches 11.08 pp
on Qwen3-8B and 14.83 on Gemma-2 9B, against the 35.2 and 47.4 a model
deciding correctly in every situation it met would score — roughly a
third of what is available in each case. The gain that is there is not
refusal: when both receive the same first answer and the same challenge,
the trained model reaches the right final answer more often than the
base model does
(App. [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
so we take part of that residual to be a limit of the model rather than
of the training: dialectical competence stands on first-answer accuracy
without following from it, and a model cannot rule correctly on a
question it is not capable of getting right in the first place. Closing
the rest is what the next work has to do, and the reference policies in
§[I](#A9 "Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
are what it should be measured against.

Concluding remarks: What limits progress in language models is
increasingly not what they can do but our ability to tell when they are
right. Every remedy for that which depends on a stronger judge — a
larger model, a separate verifier, a person — inherits the limit, and
runs out exactly where it is needed most: at the frontier, where nothing
stronger is available to ask. This work shows that one part of that
judgment can be placed inside the model, and trained there with nothing
more capable than the model being trained. It is one part and not the
whole of it, and the part still missing is the one that matters most —
because a model that could reliably feel the force of an argument it had
raised against itself would not merely be arguing well; it would be
supervising itself. We take that to be the direction this line of work
points, and the standard by which it should be judged.

## AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to implement methods: the
training and evaluation code, in addition to running and monitoring jobs
on our GPU cluster. Code implementation was restricted to decisions the
authors had already taken, not the design of the method or of the
experiments it is evaluated in. We have reviewed and verified any code
generated by AI during development, and every artifact so produced was
read and tested by the authors before any result derived from it entered
this paper. We have not used generative AI tools to develop the
conceptual framing of this work, to propose or refine its hypotheses, to
design or give feedback on its methodology or experiments, to generate
synthetic data sets, to clean or reformat the training data, to assist
with translation, to support qualitative or thematic analysis of our
data, or to interpret results; the proof-related tasks, formulating
mathematical claims, providing critical ingredients for proofs, and
writing proofs, are not applicable to this work, which contains no
theorems. Generative models also appear inside the work itself rather
than as authoring tools, as the challengers the method is trained and
evaluated against and as the blinded jury of
§[G](#A7 "Appendix G Construct validation of the primary metric ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
that reads model reasoning and judges whether a concession was genuine;
both are described in the paper as objects of study. Additionally, we
used generative AI tools to edit the text of this paper for readability;
and we have not used them to draft sections of this paper or to find
related work. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: the analysis, the
claims and the limits placed on them are the authors’ own. We take
responsibility for the final content of this work, including text,
claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

## Appendix A Related work

A large line assumes self-criticism is at worst harmless: Self-Refine
iterates critique-and-revise with no external verifier ([Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30)); Reflexion carries verbal self-reflection across
attempts ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib38)); ReVISE corrects its own
reasoning errors at test time ([Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)). Our
results show the opposite: a base model abandons more correct answers
under its own antithesis than if ignored, and reviewing its answer once
does not repair this (the answer stays the same in 95 % of cases), which
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows is not a matter of compute. SCoRe trains a single model to answer,
then to look again and decide for itself whether it erred, and it does
get a better answer, improving accuracy at both attempts ([Kumar et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21)). However well that second pass is trained, the
setting is still question and answer, with nothing put against the
answer for the model to rule on. *Dialectical competence* is a different
skill, telling a sound position from an unsound one and acting on that,
and a better answer does not buy it however much better the answer gets.
Our own arms show it directly, since the one given the same revision
pass and the one trained for accuracy alone both raise the first answer
and gain no skill. SCoRe itself, trained on our data, is compared with
our arms throughout (details in
App. [N](#A14 "Appendix N SCoRe, implemented as a trained baseline ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

The nearest line studies how a model responds when its answer is
challenged, and four works share part of our target. In the FlipFlop
experiment, [Laban et al. (2023)](#bib.bib22) follow a model’s answer
with a challenge such as “Are you sure?”, find that models often give up
correct answers, and fine-tune them to keep a correct answer and correct
a wrong one. With persuasion-balanced training (PBT), [Stengel-Eskin
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib40) train a model to resist persuasion toward a
wrong answer and to accept persuasion toward a right one, score both
directions, and show that training either side alone over-corrects.
App. [R](#A18 "Appendix R PBT’s released model in our setting ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
measures its released model in our setting. [Wang et al.
(2023a)](#bib.bib42) have a simulated user, played by ChatGPT, argue for
an invalid solution once the model has answered correctly: ChatGPT and
GPT-4 often agree with it, and for ChatGPT how often is only weakly
related to its confidence, the share of its sampled answers that are
right. S²R trains a model with reinforcement learning to verify each of
its own solutions and to try again when its verdict is negative, and in
one variant rewards each verdict by whether it is right ([Ma et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)).

Each differs from ours in design. The challenge in FlipFlop carries no
content, so the right action never depends on it, and its fine-tuning
targets are gold-labeled conversations; in our setup the nearest to it,
though not a re-implementation, is CAD-RL
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
PBT differs in why, how and what it trains. It aims to defend models
against persuasion about short factual answers on trivia and to make
teams of models work better; ours aims at a decision about an argument
on multi-step problems. It learns offline, by supervised fine-tuning and
then preference optimization, on dialogues generated once by fixed
models (for one of its runs, partly by the base model being trained),
with answers read and disagreements filtered by other language models;
ours learns online from verifiable rewards, against opposition the
policy writes as it trains, and every label is computed by a program.
And by its own analysis, PBT teaches a model “to compare the likelihood
of different answers and adopt the most likely one” (their §1, on the
analysis in their §5); our reward pays for the correctness of the
decision itself, through a verdict on the case made for the other
answer, scored against the reference like the final answer. [Wang et al.
(2023a)](#bib.bib42) train nothing, and their opposing case is always
wrong, chosen with the answer key, so yielding is not tested; our
antithesis never sees the reference and may be right, and both holding
and yielding are scored. Their finding on confidence is an observation;
our arms trained for accuracy test a related claim directly: they answer
better on the first attempt and gain no skill
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The verdict in S²R is on the model’s own solution, with no case put
against it, and its first stage learns from verifications written by
stronger models; ours rules on a case against the model’s answer and
needs no other model. Our target is a decision about an argument: the
model must reach a solution to a multi-step problem and then weigh a
worked case against it, which may be right or wrong, before it answers.
The design is chosen so that this can be learned wherever answers can be
checked: the opposition is written by the policy as it trains, so it
follows the model’s own current answers and needs no second model, and
every label comes from the verifier, so no dialogues, verifications or
preferences have to be generated or labelled in advance.

A related line asks what reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards
actually buys, and finds it raises pass@1 without lifting the
reasoning-capacity ceiling — sampling efficiency rather than new
capacity ([Yue et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)). A nearer line prices a
property that objective misses by holding the trace against a *second*
model: whether a reasoning prefix still carries a separate model to the
right answer ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib24)). It stays inside reasoning
that *reaches* an answer, and prices how well that reasoning travels. We
price a further capability: what the model does once an answer of its
own is argued against — whether it survives the challenge. Our
dissociation confirms this, and the test-time columns of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
show that sampling more answers does not produce the judgment.

A further line puts models into argument with one another: independent
instances debate to a shared answer ([Du et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)), or
two agents argue under a separate judge ([Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib25)). These are settings where the capability is exercised
rather than alternatives to it — the arguers may be copies of one model,
and what such an exchange yields depends on whether each can tell a
sound challenge from an unsound one, which is the capability a base
model is not good at. We place the opposition inside a single policy so
that the exchange can be trained on rather than only run, and so that
nothing second is needed at deployment.

A separate line studies agreement under *social* pressure: sycophancy
worsens with scale and RLHF ([Sharma et al., 2023](#bib.bib37)), and can
be reduced by fine-tuning on synthetic data that decouples an answer
from the user’s stated view ([Wei et al., 2023](#bib.bib46)). That
pressure usually carries no content, and we measure exactly that case:
Content-Agnostic Disagreement replaces the antithesis with a fixed
passage that objects without naming a defect, and it recovers roughly a
third to a half of the gain. Contentless opposition buys part of the
gain and not the whole of it — the rest requires the opposition to be
about something, which is also what makes the verdict on it checkable
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
a judgment about the argument rather than about who is making it.

A parallel line assumes supervising the trace is the lever: a process
reward model outperforms an outcome-only model at selecting correct
solutions ([Lightman et al., 2023](#bib.bib26); [Uesato et al.,
2022](#bib.bib41)); later work automates this step-level supervision to
train the policy directly ([Wang et al., 2023b](#bib.bib43)), and recent
verifiers write a verification chain of thought of their own ([Khalifa
et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Step-level or outcome-level, the target is
the same: a more accurate answer. Dialectical competence rests on it — a
model that cannot reach the right answer has nothing to hold.

## Appendix B Reproduction and artifacts

Models and hardware: Arms are trained on two base models, Qwen3-8B and
Gemma-2 9B, each on one node of eight B200 GPUs; the two recipes are
identical except for the prompt budget and the decoding during training,
given below. Rewards come from exact-match verification against the
reference answer: there is no learned reward model and no preference
data anywhere in the pipeline.

The arms: Every arm trains the same base model on the same data with the
same verifier, and differs in one respect.

- •
  *SelfD-RL* (Self-Disagreement) runs the full exchange — thesis, an
  antithesis sampled from the model’s own weights, then a verdict and a
  synthesis — and is rewarded on the synthesis.
- •
  *Accuracy-RL* takes a single pass, rewarded on whether that answer is
  right, with no exchange at all.
- •
  *Revise-RL* trains a second pass at its own answer, rewarded on the
  one it settles on and penalized for abandoning a correct one, but with
  nothing disagreeing with it there is no valid challenge to refuse; it
  is a revision control trained in one stage, without the two stages and
  the progress bonus of SCoRe, which is an arm of its own
  (App. [N](#A14 "Appendix N SCoRe, implemented as a trained baseline ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
- •
  *Verify-RL* has the model judge its own answer first and then answer
  again: the verdict is required and rewarded alongside the answer, but
  there is no opposition to rule on.
- •
  *CAD-RL* runs the same exchange against a challenge that does not
  depend on the answer it challenges.
- •
  *ExtD-RL* is the same recipe with the antithesis drawn from Qwen3-14B,
  a larger model of the same family, rather than from the model’s own
  weights.
- •
  *Majority Vote* and *Test-Time Self-Reflection* are not trained at
  all; they spend additional inference on the base model: a vote over 64
  sampled answers, or one review of its own answer.

The training data, and how it is selected: The pool is a fixed mixture
of eight verifiable-reasoning datasets — StrategyQA ([Geva et al.,
2021](#bib.bib10)), OlympiadBench ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)),
MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)), CRUXEval-O ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)), GPQA-Diamond ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib34)),
MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib16); [Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)), AMC ([AI-MO, 2024](#bib.bib2)) and
ARC-Challenge ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib4)) — 2,629 training and 327
validation questions, disjoint by construction; every comparison we
report is the same items scored before and after training, so any
overlap a benchmark may have with pretraining data enters both sides and
cancels. Training questions are then admitted by difficulty, once and
offline: for each question the frozen base model’s pass rate $`p_{0}`$
is measured from 32 samples, and only questions with
$`p_{0}\in(0.05,0.6]`$ are kept — hard enough that correction is the
common event, easy enough that the right answer is reachable under
sampling, since a question the model cannot answer at all gives it no
position to hold. That leaves 476 of the 2,629. The validation split is
never filtered, so the probe stays comparable across arms. No reward
term references $`p_{0}`$ at training time.

Optimization: GRPO with group size $`8`$, global batch $`128`$,
advantages normalized within group. Actor learning rate
$`1.0\!\times\!10^{-6}`$, constant, no warmup, weight decay $`0.01`$.
Asymmetric clipping, $`0.2`$ low and $`0.28`$ high, with dual-clip
$`c=3.0`$; entropy coefficient $`0.001`$; token-mean loss aggregation.
KL is applied as a *reward* penalty at a fixed coefficient of $`0.001`$,
not as a loss term. Rollouts are sampled, $`8`$ per prompt, at
temperature $`1.0`$ for the Qwen models and $`0.7`$ for the other
families; validation during training decodes greedily for the Qwen
models and at temperature $`0.5`$ for the others. Every arm of a family
shares these settings, except SCoRe’s KL penalties and advantage
estimator, which follow its recipe
(App. [N](#A14 "Appendix N SCoRe, implemented as a trained baseline ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Context length $`12{,}288`$ tokens ($`8{,}192`$ for Gemma-2 9B) with
responses capped at $`4{,}096`$. Rollouts are generated with vLLM.

Decoding at evaluation: The evaluated model decodes greedily unless a
result is reported over draws. A draw samples its answers at temperature
$`1.0`$ (top-p $`1.0`$) and its own antithesis at $`0.7`$ (top-p
$`0.8`$). Challengers we serve ourselves sample as its antithesis does;
challengers reached through an API are asked for temperature $`0.7`$ and
otherwise decode at their provider’s defaults.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
samples only the antithesis. On the ladder
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and
Tables [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
[8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"))
and in
Table [12](#A16.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix P Repeated challenge ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
the first answer is frozen from a greedy pass and the model’s own
antithesis is greedy.
Tables [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Validity and generalization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E The reward ablation, and the same dissociation within one arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
read training-time validation.

The reporting point: Every arm is read at a converged step: an arm whose
curve is still rising is not yet comparable, so training continues until
it flattens. Among converged checkpoints the arms are then read at a
*common step* rather than at each arm’s own peak, since reading every
arm where it happens to peak confounds the recipe with training
duration. On Qwen3-8B convergence has occurred by step $`250`$ and all
main-table arms are read there, with two exceptions recorded in the
artifact inventory rather than chosen after the fact: Accuracy-RL and
Revise-RL are read at step $`275`$, the point at which those runs were
exported. The Gemma-2 9B arms converge earlier, as
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows, so they are not trained further.

How the training curves are drawn: The lines in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
are smoothed for display — a centered rolling mean over three points,
with monotone interpolation between them — so a value read off the plot
is the smoothed one rather than a measured step. The smoothing is
presentational only: the unsmoothed series exist alongside it, and no
number reported anywhere in this paper is taken from the drawn line.

The disagreement probe: Behavior under disagreement is measured on the
disagreement probe, a fixed set of 327 items drawn from the validation
split and never trained on. Every arm sees the same items, and a draw is
scored only where the item graded cleanly under both the first answer
and the final one; that gradable count, not the number of items
challenged, is the denominator of every rate in this paper.

## Appendix C The prompts, verbatim

This appendix prints every prompt used in the three-turn exchange.
Inside the boxes a line break marked $`\hookrightarrow`$ is the
typesetter’s, introduced only to fit the column; every *unmarked* break,
and every blank line, belongs to the prompt. The templates are
reproduced from the configuration the runs read, not retyped, so what is
printed here is what executed.

### C.1 The answering turn

The answering role receives one user message and no system message. The
message is built at dataset-preparation time, not at rollout time, from

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

where `{fmt}` is selected per item from the item’s grader type. Four
distinct clauses are in use across five grader types — numeric and boxed
share one — and each is printed in full rather than elided, so every
variant can be copied:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The answer format is therefore imposed by us, and it is load-bearing
rather than cosmetic: an unparseable answer at this turn is a scored
quantity in the reward, and the later turns can refer to the format
briefly precisely because it was established here.

No system message is added on this turn, and none is injected by the
chat template of either base model. We note this because it is
model-specific: the Qwen3 template adds no default persona, whereas the
Qwen2.5 template does, and this work trains Qwen3.

### C.2 The challenging turn

The challenging role is given the system message "You're a helpful
assistant. " (the apostrophe is a plain ASCII apostrophe, and the string
ends with a space) followed by the problem and the answer under
challenge. A single challenger string is used throughout: across every
cached run of every arm in both families, the challenger role, its
opening instruction and its per-turn instruction each take exactly one
value.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One mechanical difference is worth stating for reproduction. The gemma-2
chat template rejects a system role, so the system message is folded
into the first user turn for that family. The text is the same; the
rendered message list is not, and a reproducer comparing message lists
across the two families will see that difference and should not read it
as a change of protocol.

### C.3 The revising turn

Two templates are used at the revising turn, and which one an arm
trained with depends on whether that arm was trained to return a verdict
on the challenge. The plain variant asks only for a revised answer:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The verdict variant additionally requires an explicit assessment of the
challenge before the revised answer:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ C.3 The revising turn ‣ Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
records which template each published arm was trained with. Three arms
replace the challenge itself rather than the instruction around it, and
their substituted text is given below.

| Arm         | Family   | Trained with                           | Evaluated with  |
|-------------|----------|----------------------------------------|-----------------|
| SelfD-RL    | both     | verdict variant                        | verdict variant |
| Verify-RL   | both     | self-verify-and-revise                 | verdict variant |
| CAD-RL      | Qwen3-8B | verdict variant, substituted challenge | verdict variant |
| Accuracy-RL | both     | none (single pass)                     | verdict variant |
| Revise-RL   | both     | self-revise                            | verdict variant |
| SCoRe       | both     | SCoRe’s own second attempt             | verdict variant |

Table 5: Which revising-turn template each arm was *trained* with,
resolved from the run configuration of each arm rather than from the
launcher scripts. Every arm is *evaluated* with the verdict variant, so
for Verify-RL, Accuracy-RL, Revise-RL and SCoRe the training and
evaluation prompts differ. This is deliberate: a single measurement
protocol is what allows the columns of a result table to be read as
differences in what each arm was trained to do rather than in how each
was measured.

The challenge is the situation under test, so every arm meets it, the
base model included; the arms trained without a challenge cannot be
evaluated under their own training prompts, since these contain none.
What the shared instruction adds for them is the request for a verdict,
and removing it does not help them: evaluated on the same weights and
the D-probe with the plain variant instead, each arm trained without a
challenge, and the base model, does worse on Qwen3-8B, its capitulation
6.6 to 7.3 points higher and its synthesis accuracy 4.9 to 6.2 points
lower, while on Gemma-2 9B no arm gains beyond its spread across
training seeds and the base model loses 5.4 points of synthesis
accuracy.

#### Revise-RL.

The arm receives no challenge at all; the opposing text is replaced by
an instruction to re-read its own answer. The template is the arm:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Verify-RL.

The same substitution, with the verdict step retained, so that the arm
isolates the verdict from the opposition:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### CAD-RL.

The instruction is unchanged; the challenge is replaced by a fixed
passage that objects without naming a defect, so that the arm carries
the pressure of being contradicted without carrying any information:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The passage proposes no answer, so the grader scores it as an incorrect
challenge on every rollout, $`\mathcal{V}(A;y^{\star})=0`$, and each
term of
eq. ([4](#S3.E4 "In 3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"))
that reads the challenge follows from that: the verdict is paid only for
judging the challenge incorrect, $`\beta=2.0`$ whenever the thesis is
wrong, the stubbornness penalty never applies since no challenge is
right, and the capitulation penalty applies as in Self-Disagreement.
What CAD-RL removes is therefore the content of the challenge together
with the supervision that only a challenge with an answer can give,
since a challenge that proposes nothing can be neither right nor wrong.

removed to 0.7217 with the full reward: 4.4 times as far. *And the

also holds the joint-highest thesis accuracy, so nothing here is bought
````
