What each comparison isolates: The lower panel of
Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix E The reward ablation, and the same dissociation within one arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
makes the single-setting pairs explicit. Three pairs differ in one
setting of the return: *Full return + coherence credit* and its gated
form, in the gate; the same row and SelfD-RL, in the coherence credit;
and Judge and SelfD-RL in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
in the verdict’s payment ($`w_{v}`$ 0 against 0.4). Turning the verdict
on, from *Full return, no verdict* to *Full return + coherence credit*,
adds three things at once: the requirement to give a verdict, its
payment and the coherence credit. The requirement alone is *Full return,
no verdict* against Judge: without a verdict the two verdict weights pay
nothing, so the two returns differ only in the requirement, which brings
with it the verdict template and a format gate that also checks the
verdict. From *Outcome only* to *Full return, no verdict*, the shaping
is added: $`\beta`$, both penalties and the format gate.

The weight on stubbornness sets the operating point: Two runs of
SelfD-RL trained with $`\lambda_{\mathrm{stub}}`$ raised from 0.5 to 2
(its format-gate floor moves with it, to $`-2.25`$) and read on the
disagreement probe with the base model’s exchange
(Table [14](#A17.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"))
hold 5.3 points less and yield 6.5 points more than SelfD-RL, with their
mean unchanged ($`+0.6`$, $`[-0.3,+1.6]`$) and a log odds ratio lower by
0.18 $`[0.08,0.29]`$, still above the base model’s and those of the arms
trained without a verdict. The penalty weights set where the model
stands between holding and yielding.

Within one arm over training: The second instrument reads the same
dissociation the other way, within one arm and over training rather than
across a panel at one step: dialectical competence does not arrive with
thesis accuracy, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it.
Accuracy-RL, which removes the dialectic entirely and trains single-pass
on answer correctness, raises the quantity it optimizes — 67.6 % to
71.4 % over the run — while the rate at which it surrenders a correct
answer under challenge *rises* from 31.8 % to 38.9 % over 290 steps.
Endpoints alone would prove nothing, since adjacent checkpoints swing,
so the trend is what we test: across 30 checkpoints the contrast is
$`+4.4`$ pp (95 % CI $`[+1.5,+7.5]`$ pp) and the slope $`+1.3`$ pp per
hundred steps, both excluding zero under a question-clustered bootstrap.
This is a single dissociation and the spread is not certified
equivalent.
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 The problem ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows the consequence on held-out benchmarks — Accuracy-RL moves to the
right and not upward.

## Appendix F What the opposition and the verdict do in training

Whether the disagreement must carry real content, and whether it must
come from elsewhere, is answered in the body by three controls that do
not depend on this section: removing the *content* of the disagreement,
with the supervision that depends on it
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
costs roughly half to two thirds of the gain, sourcing the disagreement
from a separate model lands within the same interval
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
and the trained model keeps its advantage against almost every one of
the fifteen challengers it never trained against
(Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
Nothing below is a substitute for those: a rate at which the opposition
disagrees cannot by itself distinguish a real challenge from a staged
one, because both produce disagreement. What this section adds is a
description of what the opposition and the verdict actually do inside
training.

Three provisions in
§[3](#S3 "3 Design ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
bear on trivial agreement — the two outside the objective, an uninformed
opposing role and the admission band, and a $`\beta`$ that prices
correction on the one cell where deference cannot produce a correct
answer. None of them guarantees it. This section reports what the
opposition and the verdict actually do.

The opposition disagrees, and is sometimes right: Over 256,000
dialectical exchanges in training, the opposition proposed a different
answer from the thesis often enough for both responses to be exercised,
arriving at a correct answer on 43 % of items where the thesis was
already correct and 38 % of those where it was not.

The verdict is more than agreement: Nothing in the objective forces the
verdict to be informative: a policy that returns agreement whenever the
opposition happens to agree collects the same credit. What separates the
two is whether the verdict follows a base rate *that moves*. The trained
policy credits the opposition on 41.8 % of training items against a true
rate of 39.5 %, and on 62.00 % against 60.40 % on a held-out probe whose
true rate is more than twenty pp away, while the arm paid only for its
first answer, with no verdict in training (Unrew.,
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")),
is off by 24 and 17 pp respectively. The argument rests on the verdict
following a base rate that moves, not on the exact figures.

## Appendix G Construct validation of the primary metric

The rubric: Each item presents one complete trace — problem, initial
solution, the challenge to it, and the revised solution — and asks for
two integer scores. The first, *was the challenge substantive?*, is
binary, and it is deliberately strict: a generic expression of doubt
scores zero, and so does a challenge that ends on the same final answer
as the initial solution, no matter how much text it contains, because it
does not actually oppose. The second, *was the revised solution genuine
reasoning?*, runs zero to three, where zero is conceding and adopting
the challenge’s answer with no valid pushback, or merely restating the
challenge. Scores of zero or one are treated as non-genuine. The second
score is the primary one; the first characterizes the input the policy
was reacting to.

Blinding: The judge is instructed that it is blind to which answer is
correct and told not to attempt to determine it. The reference answer is
never shown. Neither is the arm, the model identity, nor which outcome
cell the item was drawn from, so a judge cannot infer what the item is
supposed to demonstrate. Answers are presented in neutral roles —
initial solution, challenge, revised solution — rather than by their
origin.

Panel and agreement: The panel is Claude-Opus-4.7, GPT-5.5 and
Gemini-3.1-pro-preview, uniform across every trace, with no exclusions,
no unparsable responses and no truncated inputs. Inter-judge reliability
is Krippendorff’s $`\alpha`$, an agreement coefficient corrected for
chance where $`1`$ is perfect agreement and $`0`$ is chance: 0.936 on
the antithesis judgment and 0.789 on the genuineness judgment, both
computed on the ordinal scale. On the capitulation stratum, scoring by
mean rather than by majority returns the identical count, so the
headline does not depend on the aggregation rule. The verdicts do not
hinge on the panel’s members: a second panel of newer models,
Claude-Opus-5.5, GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini-4-argon, given the same prompt
on 300 of these traces, 75 from each of the four strata, agrees with
this one at $`\alpha=0.93`$ on the mean genuineness score, computed on
squared distances rather than the ordinal scale, and also judges every
capitulation non-genuine; Claude-Opus-5.5 returned no answer on 20
traces, which the other two judges decide.

Grading the antithesis: The jury grades the antithesis as well as the
synthesis, on a deliberately strict definition: an antithesis that
voices generic doubt, or that ends on the same answer as the thesis,
counts as no opposition at all. By that standard the policy’s
self-generated antithesis is substantive in 67 % of items, so the
opposition the synthesis faces is not a formality.

Self-preference: One judge shares a developer with one of the models
whose traces are being rated. Rather than assume this away we measured
it: that judge’s offset on those items, relative to its own offset on
the rest, is $`-0.007`$ (bootstrap 95 % CI $`[-0.077,+0.068]`$). The
interval contains zero and is narrow, so there is no detectable
self-preference to correct for.

What was graded: The validity check is the base model’s capitulations
($`n=121`$), all of which the panel judged non-genuine. Three further
groups ask whether holding is genuine rather than stubborn: the base
model’s held ($`n=381`$, of which 20.2 % non-genuine) and corrected
($`n=89`$, 49.4 % non-genuine) syntheses, and the trained model’s held
syntheses ($`n=590`$). Grading both models on holding is what makes the
comparison like-for-like: on the 350 trained syntheses whose counterpart
on the base model also held, low-quality holding falls from 20.2 % to
12.6 %. A re-rated control bounds judge drift at 0.024 on the four-point
scale; it is carried with every comparison, and the one result whose
significance depends on it is stated as not detected rather than as an
effect.

What the grading does not establish: We validate only the low end of the
scale. A score of zero has an unambiguous behavioral meaning — the
synthesis concedes and adopts the antithesis’s answer with no valid
pushback, or merely restates it — whereas a high score is not a
certificate that the reasoning is sound, and we do not claim it as one.
The grading is of the *visible* reasoning in a trace, so it cannot
separate a well-reasoned synthesis from a well-presented one.
Capitulation is graded only on the base model, because training reduces
the behavior to roughly one item in seventy — too few to rate; that gap
runs in the conservative direction, since counting those residual
reversals as capitulation can only overstate what remains. Validation
used a fixed three-judge panel over more than a thousand traces from
three models — Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2 9B and Llama-3.1-8B — taken from both
the base and the trained checkpoint of each.

## Appendix H What the trained model leaves on the table, across challengers

This is a separate instrument from
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and should not be read as a certification of it: the items on which the
base model’s first answer was correct — 221 of the D-probe’s 327 items,
the base-correct stratum as frozen for this campaign;
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
reports 223 for the same probe under its own thesis draw — held fixed,
with both arms scored on the same items against three antitheses. The
quantity is what each arm leaves on the table, the share of that
population it fails to carry through.

Why this is not three lucky numbers: A residual that barely moves across
three antitheses is easy to read as a coincidence of three numbers.
Across them the trained model’s holding rate varies less than sampling
noise alone would produce on a set this size — $`0.32\times`$ the spread
three draws would be expected to show — while the base model’s varies
more, at $`1.47\times`$. So the one column is genuinely invariant and
the other genuinely moves. Training does not remove a fixed share of the
damage; it removes whatever is needed to arrive at the same place.

Table 9: The dialectical profile. For each of the four situations,
$`\pi`$ is the share of gradable item-draws that fall in it and $`r`$ is
how often the model then ends on the correct answer;
$`c_{S}=\sum_{m}\pi_{m}r_{m}`$, which the table reproduces up to the
rounding shown. Situations are defined by the model’s own first answer
and its challenger’s, so $`r`$ is a rate within that arm’s own cell and
is read together with the $`\pi`$ beside it. All shares over one
denominator, the same for every arm to within 0.4 %; trained arms are
the mean of three training seeds. 16 external challengers plus the
model’s own critique. *hold* and *yield* are the situations with a side
to choose; *keep* is a correct agreement already in hand; *new* is the
one where neither answer was right and the chance level is exactly zero.

The profile in full:
Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
gives all four situations. The two with a side to choose carry the
result: the base models yield far more often than they hold, and the
model trained with Self-Disagreement holds in about nine cases in ten
and still yields in about half. The third situation, where both answers
were already right, is at ceiling for every arm and separates nothing.
The fourth is the one whose chance level is exactly zero, since neither
answer contains the solution and only a new one can succeed; every arm,
ours included, remains poor there, and it is the clearest statement of
what the method does not yet do.

Why the distance and not the level: Each situation is defined by which
answer was right, so on the first a policy that simply keeps its first
answer is right on every item by construction, and on the second a
policy that simply takes the challenger’s is. Those policies ignore the
exchange entirely. No arm beats them here and none could; what separates
the arms is how much of that free score each one gives away by engaging
at all.

The holding half separates, and only for one arm: The base model gives
away 46.7 of the hundred points it would have scored by keeping its
first answer, and on Gemma it gives away 74.9. The trained rivals stay
close to that: they give away between 50.0 and 51.5 on Qwen, and between
71.1 and 78.9 on Gemma. Self-Disagreement gives away 11.1 and 10.5. It
is also highest in level against almost every challenger we ran across
the two models. The rivals are the control that matters here: each of
them also raises first-answer accuracy, and none of them converts that
into keeping a position under challenge.

The same result read as a spread: What separates the arms is not only
how often they end on the correct side but how much that depends on
which challenger they faced. Read across challengers — and read only on
the ones every arm faced, since a rung one arm skipped would widen
another’s span for free — the base model’s rate of holding a right first
answer on Qwen spans 56 pp over seventeen challengers, from its weakest
rung to its strongest, while Self-Disagreement spans 11. On Gemma, over
seventeen challengers, 57 against 15. *The trained rivals stay wide*:
they span 48–51 on Qwen and 52–62 on Gemma, in both families nearer the
base model’s spread than Self-Disagreement’s. Raising first-answer
accuracy buys a few pp of level and no independence from who is arguing.

That is also the answer to the obvious objection: A model that had
merely learned not to move would sit *at* the keep-your-answer policy
rather than 11.1 and 10.5 pp below it, and would not still be moving on
the second population, where it ends on the correct side 53.3 % and
55.4 % of the time. Engaging costs it something; it is not declining to
engage.

Both halves are counted in one number: Self-Disagreement yields
correctly less often than the base model, and 46.7 and 44.6 pp less
often than the ignore-the-exchange policy on Qwen and Gemma. That fall
sits inside the *skill* term, which sums over all four situations, so
the gain reported there is already net of it. The base model’s own
pairing is what that is measured against: that model ends on the correct
side of 93.2 % of Gemma’s yielding items while managing only 25.1 % of
its holding items, which is not discrimination but near-unconditional
surrender, and the same behavior produces both numbers.

## Appendix J Test-time compute baselines

How the test-time columns of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
were produced: Two schemes stand in for spending more at inference
rather than training differently. *Majority vote* draws 64 synthesis
samples for an item and returns the modal answer, which is
self-consistency ([Wang et al., 2022](#bib.bib44)). In *self-reflection*
the base model answers, meets its own antithesis and gives its
synthesis, exactly as in the Base column; it is then asked once to
review and update that answer, one round of self-refinement in the sense
of [Madaan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib30). Each question gets eight such
samples, one from each of the Base column’s sampled answers, scored
individually and averaged. Both run on the base model, on the same
items, scored by the same verifier as every other column. Neither
reaches the capability the paper is about: on Qwen3-8B, majority voting
raises the average from 50.0 to 52.2 and self-reflection leaves it at
50.1, against 55.9 for Self-Disagreement. On the D-probe, the same
review keeps the base model’s answer in 95 % of the 2616 item-draws.

The one difference a reader must know about: Every column of that table
samples at the same temperature, these two included. What differs is the
spread of majority vote: it already aggregates 64 samples internally, so
the variation left across its three draws is smaller than the
single-sample columns’ for reasons that have nothing to do with how
stable the method is. Self-reflection is scored like the Base column,
one sample for each of the same eight sampled answers.

Estimator: Rates are reported in the *joint* form over all scored items
($`n=2616`$), never as a per-arm conditional rate, and intervals are
clustered by question (327 clusters), because repeats of one item are
not independent observations. Call counts are reported to say what was
spent and are *not* offered as a cost comparison.

## Appendix K Pre-registrations and outcome commitments

Two quantities in this paper were fixed before the runs that report them
existed, because each is a place where a margin chosen afterwards would
decide its own outcome.

Non-inferiority under challenge: Before any further challenger arm
executed, we fixed the primary challenger as gpt-5-mini and the
non-inferiority margin at $`\delta=0.05`$ on the accuracy scale, and
committed to reporting the result whichever way it fell. The question is
whether a model’s accuracy under challenge stays within $`\delta`$ of
its accuracy unchallenged. Self-Disagreement passes: the interval on the
difference is $`[-0.015,+0.061]`$, whose lower bound clears the margin —
non-inferiority is one-sided, so only that end is at issue. The base
model fails, and not marginally — $`[-0.288,-0.135]`$, wholly below the
margin. *The margin was fixed while we still did not know which arms
would clear it.*

Cross-family transfer: We committed in advance to reporting the second
base model on the same panel and at the same reporting point as the
first, whatever it showed, rather than selecting a family after seeing
the result. One outcome of that commitment is disclosed in
§[L](#A12 "Appendix L The second base model, benchmark by benchmark ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and is not flattering: on the second family one benchmark is near zero
for every arm and carries no reading at all.

## Appendix M Reward-hacking controls

The reward pays for correcting a flawed first answer, which creates an
obvious exploit: degrade the first answer so that there is always
something to correct. The exploit is real and has been observed in this
codebase, so we treat it as a check that must pass rather than as an
objection to be argued away.

The first answer is not sacrificed: Compared at matched steps,
first-answer accuracy does not fall in the dialectical arms. *This is a
control and not a result:* training raises it in every arm including the
unrewarded-dialectic one, so it does not distinguish the treatment and
no claim in this paper rests on it.

The synthesis is not copied from the challenge: The sharper check,
because it tests the route by which a gain could be manufactured. The
rate at which the final answer simply reproduces the challenger’s falls
from $`0.693`$ in the unrewarded-dialectic arm to $`0.393`$–$`0.419`$ in
the arms that pay for the verdict. *The arms that defend better are the
arms that copy less*, so the gain cannot be attributed to adopting the
challenge more often. The arm with the verdict term removed sits at
$`0.705`$, with the control rather than the treatment, which is the
internal check that the effect follows the variable we manipulated.

No format exploitation: Pooled over each training run, format-failure
rates are below $`2`$ % on both the first and the final answer in every
arm, except SCoRe’s first attempt on Gemma-2 9B (4.8–5.4 %), so the
route in which a reward is captured by malformed output is not active.

What these checks do not establish: They are a conjunction, and they are
one-sided. The opposite failure — refusing a challenge that deserved to
be accepted — passes every check above, which is why it is priced
directly in the objective and measured separately rather than left to
these controls.

## Appendix N SCoRe, implemented as a trained baseline

SCoRe ([Kumar et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) trains a single model to
correct its own answer with reinforcement learning: the model answers,
is told that its solution may contain an error, and answers again, with
no opposing argument and no verdict. It is the published recipe closest
to Revise-RL, which also revises without opposition, so we implemented
it on our setup and trained it on both base models.
Tables [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")–[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Where the gain comes from ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
and [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")–[14](#A17.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
carry it beside the other arms, read with exactly their protocol.

The recipe as we ran it: Each training trajectory has two turns. The
first is our thesis prompt, the question with its answer format, as for
every arm. The second appends SCoRe’s instruction to look again (*“There
might be an error in the solution above because of lack of understanding
of the question. Please correct the error, if any, and rewrite the
solution.”*), with only its answer-format clause replaced by ours.
Training has two stages, and each attempt earns $`1`$ if its final
answer is correct and $`0`$ otherwise. In Stage I only the second
attempt is rewarded, and a KL penalty of $`0.1`$ holds the first attempt
near the base model. In Stage II both attempts are rewarded, and the
second also earns a progress bonus $`\alpha\,(r_{2}-r_{1})`$ with
$`\alpha=10`$. A KL penalty of $`0.01`$ applies to every turn in both
stages, and, as for every arm, it enters the reward rather than the
loss. Rewards are per turn, with no discounting across turns. Each
sample’s advantage is taken against the other seven samples of its
prompt (RLOO), inside the clipped update of
§[B](#A2 "Appendix B Reproduction and artifacts ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement").
Data, initialization, verifier, learning rate, batch, group size and
training decoding are those of every arm on the same base model.
Stage II starts from Stage I’s weights and position in the data, with a
fresh optimizer state. Qwen3-8B trains for $`250`$ steps, $`125`$ in
each stage, and Gemma-2 9B for $`100`$, $`50`$ in each; each seed is
read at its last step, the common step of its base model.

## Appendix P Repeated challenge

Every result in the main text comes from a single round of challenge: a
first answer, one antithesis and one synthesis. A model that holds once
could still give way when the challenge is repeated, so this appendix
asks whether the gain survives further rounds. After three rounds,
Self-Disagreement still has the highest synthesis accuracy on both base
models, and it is right in all three rounds far more often than any
other arm
(Table [12](#A16.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix P Repeated challenge ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Setup: Round 1 is the dialectic on a D-probe item: the model answers,
writes its own antithesis and then a synthesis. In each later round the
same model writes a new antithesis against its current answer, in a
fresh call that carries no history, and then a new synthesis that
continues the conversation, so the model sees its first answer and every
earlier challenge and synthesis. We ran three rounds on the 327 D-probe
items, sampled four times per item, with each trained arm at its three
training seeds. A round that ends without a readable answer counts as
wrong.

Result: After round 3, Self-Disagreement’s synthesis accuracy is 72.0 %
on Qwen3-8B and 52.4 % on Gemma-2 9B, against at most 64.8 % and 41.7 %
for every other arm, and it is right in all three rounds on 70.0 % and
48.1 % of items, against at most 53.9 % and 26.0 %, a lead that stays
above 13 points in every 95 % interval over items. It leads on both
measures also when each round instead starts afresh, with the previous
synthesis as the thesis.

## Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm

Every arm in the upper block of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
meets its own antithesis, so its synthesis accuracy reflects both how it
decides and what it is asked to decide on. Holding the challenge fixed
separates the two: every arm receives the same first answer and the same
antithesis from an outside model, and only the decision is its own. The
lead survives on both base models and against both challengers
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
lower block), and
Table [13](#A17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
shows why: the arms trained on other objectives, and the base model
given more inference, answer an antithesis much as the base model does,
taking most of them whether right or wrong, while Self-Disagreement
holds against the wrong ones and still takes most of the right ones, and
the base model made to switch as rarely does not catch up, so the
advantage lies in which items it holds on, not in how many.

Setup: For every item of the panel (38,434 per base model, GPQA on its
250 items), the base model’s first answer from its first run is
challenged once by Gemini-3.8-flash and once by Claude-Haiku-4.5, each
writing one antithesis with the challenging prompt of
App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C The prompts, verbatim ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
the prompt the base model itself answers. Every arm writes the synthesis
to that first answer and that antithesis with the harness, template and
decoding of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"),
each trained arm at its three training seeds and the base model, each
with eight sampled syntheses per item; Self-Refl reviews each of those
eight syntheses once, and Maj@64 is drawn three separate times, each
draw the majority answer of 64 sampled syntheses. Only the synthesis is
sampled. The outside antithesis is right on 36.2 and 46.1 % of the items
against Qwen3-8B’s first answers and on 40.5 and 33.1 % against
Gemma-2 9B’s (Gemini-3.8-flash and Claude-Haiku-4.5, in that order; mean
over the benchmarks).

Deciding, not yielding less: On the items where exactly one of the first
answer and the antithesis is right, the right decision is known, and an
arm that only yields less trades one kind of error for the other.
Self-Disagreement does more than that: it holds where holding is right
on 45 to 78 % of these items, against 5 to 31 % for every other arm,
while still yielding where yielding is right on 70 to 80 %, against 84
to 99 %, so the mean of the two rates puts it 8 to 19 points above every
other arm, and the AUC of its switching (the probability that an item
where the antithesis is right draws more switches than one where it is
wrong, ties counting half) is the highest in every cell (0.68 to 0.88,
against at most 0.81 for any other arm).

More inference sharpens what the base model already does: Taking the
majority of 64 samples turns the base model’s lean toward the antithesis
into its answer, so it holds even less where holding is right (5 to
22 %) and yields even more where yielding is right (94 to 99 %), leaving
its mean of the two rates within 3.5 points of the base model’s. A
single review of each synthesis leaves Qwen3-8B where it was and costs
Gemma-2 9B 4 to 5 points. Neither supplies what training on the
challenge does, which is the conclusion the upper block of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Overall results and analysis ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
reaches with each arm’s own antithesis.

Switching less is not what makes it better: Self-Disagreement switches
on fewer of these items than the base model, but making the base model
switch as rarely does not make it decide as well. Pushed toward holding
at its verdict word (biases fixed in advance, up to 16 in log-odds), the
base model changes its verdict and not its answer, and never comes down
to Self-Disagreement’s switch rate; pushed at its final answer, it does
come down to it on Gemma-2 9B against both challengers, and there
Self-Disagreement’s mean of the two rates is still higher by 10.4 and
7.0 points (95 % intervals $`[9.1,11.9]`$ and $`[4.7,9.5]`$), and its
synthesis accuracy by 7.5 and 4.4. On Qwen3-8B the pushes fixed in
advance do not bring the base model down to that rate; larger ones added
afterwards (32 and 64, read from the same samples) do, against both
challengers, and there Self-Disagreement’s mean of the two rates is
higher by 17.7 and 9.9 points ($`[15.3,18.7]`$ and $`[7.6,11.9]`$) and
its synthesis accuracy by 12.4 and 8.3. On both base models, then, its
advantage lies in which items it holds on, not in how many.

The disagreement probe, with the base model’s exchange for every arm:
The same design on the probe of
§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement"):
every arm receives the base model’s first answer to each of its 327
questions and the antithesis each of the seventeen challengers of
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I The challenger probe, rung by rung ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
wrote against it, and writes eight syntheses per training run
(Table [14](#A17.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement");
95 % intervals resample the questions, with the eight draws fixed). With
the exchange fixed, the odds ratios of
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Validity and generalization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
can be compared across models. Self-Disagreement’s log odds ratio is
above the base model’s by 0.68 $`[0.40,0.98]`$ on Qwen3-8B and 1.23
$`[0.89,1.56]`$ on Gemma-2 9B, and above each of Verify-RL, Revise-RL,
Accuracy-RL and SCoRe by 0.47 to 0.66 and 0.88 to 1.12, every interval
above zero; its mean of holding and yielding is above the base model’s
by 5.1 $`[2.4,7.7]`$ and 17.2 $`[14.8,19.6]`$ points. Paying for the
verdict moves the balance toward holding: against Judge, which must give
the verdict and is not paid for it, Self-Disagreement holds 6.2 points
more $`[5.3,7.1]`$ and yields 7.6 points less $`[6.3,9.0]`$, with no
change in their mean ($`-0.7`$, $`[-1.5,+0.1]`$) and a log odds ratio
higher by 0.20 $`[0.11,0.30]`$.

Told to hold, the base model still decides worse: We also instructed the
base model to keep its first answer, at three strengths fixed in
advance, each replacing the template’s sentence “Update if the
opposition is genuinely right; defend if it is wrong” with one of
“Update only if you are confident the opposition is right; otherwise
keep your answer”, “Your first answer is usually right. Keep it unless
the opposition shows a specific error in it that you can verify” and
“Keep your first answer. Change it only if the opposition proves beyond
doubt that it is wrong”, on the probe with the base model’s exchange
(Table [14](#A17.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix Q The same challenge for every arm ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
The prompted base model still yields on 81.1 to 83.7 % of the items
where yielding is right on Qwen3-8B and 92.2 to 94.4 % on Gemma-2 9B,
against Self-Disagreement’s 58.3 and 63.0 %, and at every strength
Self-Disagreement’s mean of holding and yielding is higher, by 3.5 to
5.2 and 14.4 to 19.0 points, every interval above zero.

## Appendix R PBT’s released model in our setting

PBT ([Stengel-Eskin et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)) trains a model to accept
persuasion toward a right answer and to resist it toward a wrong one,
the two-sided target we share
(App. [A](#A1 "Appendix A Related work ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).
We measure its released model in our setting, beside the model it starts
from, Llama-3.1-8B (instruction-tuned), and SelfD-RL trained from the
same model (one training run, step 150), with the paper’s grader
(Table [15](#A18.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix R PBT’s released model in our setting ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")).

Against its own antithesis: On the disagreement probe, PBT’s synthesis
accuracy and capitulation are close to the base model’s (51.4 and 4.2 %
against 53.8 and 4.4 %), and SelfD-RL is ahead on both (58.5 and 2.2 %).
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Validity and generalization ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Benchmarks Don’t Talk Back:Learning Through Self-Disagreement")
reads the same base model on validation during training, over two seeds,
hence its different values.

Given the same exchange: With the base model’s first answer and an
outside challenger’s antithesis (Gemini-3.8-flash and Claude-Haiku-4.5),
PBT moves the base model toward holding, 15.1 points more holding and
14.7 points less yielding, with their mean level with the base model’s
($`+0.2`$ points, $`[-2.6,+2.9]`$). SelfD-RL leads PBT on the mean by
5.7 points $`[2.7,8.6]`$ and on the AUC by 0.140 $`[0.085,0.200]`$, and
the base model by 5.9 points $`[3.5,8.4]`$ and 0.114 $`[0.060,0.166]`$;
95 % intervals resample the questions, with the draws fixed. The models
were trained on different data, so this compares released models, not
methods.
